quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
quiz_item.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.

pamphlet_excerpts: Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed: Your counselor that you are able: The following are common weaves used in this pamphlet (p. 11).

Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 2: Your counselor that you are able Principle 2: Sometimes called over-under weave, the plain weave is done with rigid stakes or spokes, and weavers that wrap around the stakes in an over-one (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 3: Your counselor that you are able Principle 3: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reed than weavers (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 4: Your counselor that you are able Principle 4: Continuous weave looks much the same as plain weave, but it is woven with a different technique (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 1 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave is created over an odd number of stakes (p. 11).

Step 2 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 2 (Your counselor that you are able): It is not done one row at a time, but continuously from beginning to end, with additional weavers added when more length is needed (p. 11).

Step 3 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 3 (Your counselor that you are able): This method of weaving involves the weaver passing over two or more stakes and under two or more stakes at a time (p. 11).

Step 4 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 4 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave, sometimes called pairing, involves two weavers, each alternately twisting over and under consecutive spokes (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.
